cues.text: On the night of August 14 to 15, 1730, the people of Siena, Italy, were celebrating the eve of the Assumption.
During the festivities, thieves broke into the church of San Francesco and made off with a golden ciborium holding 351 consecrated Hosts.
The theft plunged the city into genuine mourning — even the Palio, Siena's famous horse race, was suspended as an act of civic reparation.
Three days later, on August 17, a man praying at the nearby sanctuary of Santa Maria in Provenzano noticed something unusual protruding from the church's alms box for the poor.
Inside, covered in dust, all 351 Hosts were found — every one of them accounted for and completely intact.
The city celebrated the recovery with a solemn procession carrying the Hosts back to San Francesco.

Rather than distribute or consume the recovered Hosts immediately, church authorities set them aside, expecting that unconsecrated bread of the same kind would naturally decay within a matter of years under ordinary conditions.
Decades passed, and the Hosts showed no sign of corruption at all — a state that has persisted, according to repeated examination, for nearly three centuries.

The Hosts have been formally examined multiple times by scientists and physicians, most notably in 1914 under the authorization of Pope St. Pius X. A team including chemists and pharmacologists concluded the Hosts remained fresh, chemically pure, and free of any trace of decay or artificial preservative.
Pope St. John Paul II visited Siena in 1980 to venerate the Hosts in person, reportedly remarking simply, 'It's the Presence.'

Roughly 223 of the original 351 Hosts remain preserved today in the Basilica of San Francesco, the difference accounted for by particles distributed for devotional purposes over the centuries before the remainder were set aside permanently.
Siena marks the anniversary of the recovery with Eucharistic adoration on the 17th of every month.

It also observes a solemn Corpus Christi procession and the traditional homage of the city's historic contrada districts—a devotion built not around a single dramatic moment, but around nearly three centuries of simple, sustained, and repeatedly tested absence of decay.
